content.title: About
content.content: Cabbage Salad (NFS) is a ready‑to‑eat mix of fresh white cabbage, carrot, onion and a light dressing made from vegetable oil and vinegar. The product is intended for quick preparation of a side dish or light snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cabbage is rich in vitamin C and dietary fiber, supporting immunity and digestion.
The NFS (Not From Scratch) label indicates the product is ready to eat without further processing.
The salad is frequently used in culinary schools as a base ingredient for both Asian and European dishes.
Some versions undergo a quick fermentation, helping the cabbage stay crisp longer.
Packaging is made from recyclable plastic to reduce environmental impact.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Cabbage salad is low in calories, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phytonutrients in cabbage help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Cabbage provides potassium and modest sodium levels, contributing to normal blood pressure.

items.title: Cabbage allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cabbage.

items.title: Sodium in the dressing
items.content: Certain dressing formulations contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Bacterial spoilage if stored improperly
items.content: Improper storage can lead to spoilage and potential foodborne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The salad is ready to eat straight from the package. Serve it as a snack, add it to sandwiches, use as a base for wraps, or combine with other vegetables and protein sources.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0 °C to +4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. Do not freeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken fricassee, Puerto Rican style is a traditional island dish featuring chicken simmered in a fragrant sauce of tomatoes, olive oil, garlic, onion, sweet pepper, olives, capers and spices such as oregano and adobo. It is commonly served with rice, beans and fried plantains.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The term “fricassee” comes from the French “fricassée,” meaning stewed meat without a crust.
The Puerto Rican version adds Caribbean staples like olives, capers and sweet pepper.
The dish can be prepared in a single day, but flavors deepen after a few hours or overnight refrigeration.
Traditionally young chicken (often called “pollo”) is used for its tenderness.
In Puerto Rico fricassee is a favorite for holidays and family celebrations.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When prepared without excessive butter, the dish remains moderate in saturated fat.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken supplies niacin, B6 and B12, supporting metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Tomatoes, sweet pepper and onion contain lycopene and quercetin, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Olives and capers add potassium, iron and magnesium, important for muscle and heart function.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The sauce often includes soy sauce or added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Olives and capers are salty
items.content: These ingredients can increase overall sodium, which may be unsuitable for kidney disease.

items.title: Thorough cooking required
items.content: Chicken must reach a safe internal temperature to avoid salmonella risk.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Brown chicken pieces until golden, then set aside. In the same pan sauté onion, garlic, sweet pepper, add tomatoes, olives, capers and spices. Return chicken, add a splash of broth and simmer covered 30–40 minutes until tender. Serve with rice, beans and fried plantains.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the finished dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container. Refrigerate up to 3 days. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken fajita is a Mexican‑style dish made of thin strips of chicken breast sautéed with bell peppers, onions, and spices. It is usually served with warm tortillas, salsa, guacamole, and sour cream.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Originally fajitas were made with beef, but chicken became popular for its lower calorie count.
The dish is believed to have originated in Texas in the early 20th century, cooked by Mexican laborers over open flames.
Authentic flavor comes from cumin, paprika, chili powder, and lime juice.
Fajitas are often served “build‑your‑own,” letting diners assemble their own tortillas.
In the United States, chicken fajita is one of the top‑selling items on fast‑casual Mexican menus.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with beef, chicken contains less saturated fat, making it a heart‑friendlier option.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken supplies niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Bell peppers and onions are high in vitamin C and quercetin, helping combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: The combination of lean protein and vitamins helps strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared spice mixes or sauces can add a lot of salt; monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Undercooked meat
items.content: Insufficiently cooked chicken may harbor pathogens such as Salmonella.

items.title: Spicy ingredients
items.content: Chili and other hot spices can irritate the stomach in people with sensitive digestion.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve chicken fajita in warm tortillas, topped with salsa, guacamole, sour cream, cheese, and fresh cilantro. It can be enjoyed as a main dish or added to salads and bowls.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked fajita in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat until the chicken reaches an internal temperature of 75 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Mackerel is a marine fish from the Scombridae family, known for its rich flavor and aroma. Grilled mackerel features a crispy skin and tender, fragrant flesh. It is a popular dish in many cuisines, especially around the Mediterranean and East Asia.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mackerel is high in omega‑3 fatty acids, which are beneficial for heart and brain health.
In the wild, mackerel migrates in massive schools, traveling long distances between spawning and feeding grounds.
Mackerel is used in traditional dishes such as Japanese "saba" and Spanish "sardinas en aceite".
A single mackerel can weigh up to 1.5 kg, but it is usually sold in portions of 200‑400 g.
Grilling over an open flame imparts a characteristic smoky aroma.

items.title: Rich source of omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids help lower triglyceride levels and support cardiovascular health.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Mackerel provides complete animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The fish contains vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Mackerel is a good source of selenium, phosphorus, and iodine, supporting thyroid function and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Eye health
items.content: Vitamin A and DHA in mackerel contribute to healthy vision.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: Like many larger predatory fish, mackerel can contain low levels of mercury; moderate consumption is advised, especially for children and pregnant women.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood, including mackerel.

items.title: High sodium in marinated versions
items.content: If the fish is pre‑marinated, consider the added salt in your overall diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Grilled mackerel can be served as a main dish, sliced into salads, used in sandwiches, or as part of appetizers. It pairs well with lemon, fresh herbs, and light sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep grilled mackerel refrigerated at 0 °C–4 °C in an airtight container for no more than 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Orange tomatoes are tomatoes of varieties with orange or golden-yellow skin and flesh. They have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and juicy, tender flesh. Carotenoids give them their orange color. The tomatoes are eaten fresh and added to salads, sandwiches, sauces, and salsa, or roasted and grilled.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Carotenoids, including beta-carotene and prolycopene, give tomatoes their orange color.
Tetra-cis-lycopene in orange tomatoes is absorbed by the body better than the trans-lycopene of red tomatoes.
Botanically, a tomato is a berry and is native to South and Central America.
Orange and yellow varieties often seem milder and sweeter than red ones.
Orange tomatoes make bright golden sauces and soups.

items.title: Contain carotenoids
items.content: Carotenoids have antioxidant properties, and the body converts some of them into vitamin A.

items.title: Contain vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Contain potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Contain folate
items.content: Folate is important for cell formation.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Tomatoes are low in calories and high in water.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Tomatoes can cause heartburn in people with a sensitive stomach.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Tomato allergy is possible, including in people sensitive to pollen.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: People with kidney disease who need to limit potassium should consult a doctor.

items.title: Leaves and green parts
items.content: The leaves, stems, and green parts of the tomato plant contain alkaloids and are not edible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wash tomatoes and eat them fresh, slice them into salads and sandwiches, add them to salsa, sauces, and soups, or roast and grill them. Carotenoids are absorbed better with fat, so tomatoes pair well with olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store tomatoes at room temperature away from direct sunlight until they ripen. In the refrigerator they lose flavor and texture, so use it only for ripe tomatoes you need to keep. Keep sliced tomatoes in the refrigerator for two to three days.

content.title: About
content.content: Pepperoni pizza is a popular fast‑food option consisting of a medium crust topped with tomato sauce, mozzarella cheese, and slices of spicy pepperoni sausage. It is commonly served in quick‑serve restaurants and pizzerias.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pepperoni is an American adaptation of Italian salami, created in the early 20th century.
Traditionally the pizza is baked at 250‑300 °C, producing a crisp crust.
The combination of spicy meat and melted cheese makes it one of the best‑selling pizzas in the United States.
Some regions add a pinch of sugar to the pepperoni to enhance caramelization.
Pepperoni pizza often appears in eating challenges because of its high calorie count.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Pepperoni and cheese provide high‑quality protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Mozzarella cheese is a good source of calcium, supporting bone health.

items.title: Vitamin B12
items.content: The meat component supplies vitamin B12, essential for nervous system function and blood formation.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Pepperoni contains iron, which helps transport oxygen in the bloodstream.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Its high calorie density provides quick energy, useful during intense physical activity.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Pepperoni and prepared sauces are salty, which can raise blood pressure if consumed frequently.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese and processed meat contain saturated fats that may increase cholesterol levels.

items.title: Processed meat
items.content: Processed meats are linked to higher risk of certain diseases when eaten in large amounts.

items.title: Allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to dairy or the spices used in pepperoni.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: A single slice can contain 250‑350 kcal, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pepperoni pizza is typically enjoyed hot, cut into triangular slices. Adding fresh vegetables, basil, or a drizzle of olive oil can balance the richness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore a crispy crust.

potato-skins-with-cheese-and-bacon.title: Potato skins with cheese and bacon

content.title: About
content.content: Potato skins with cheese and bacon are baked potato halves filled with shredded cheese, crispy bacon bits, and seasonings. The dish is often served as an appetizer or side, combining the creamy taste of cheese, the savory aroma of bacon, and a light crunchy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tradition of serving potato skins began in the United States in the early 1920s.
Cheddar or Monterey Jack are commonly used because they melt well.
Bacon is added as finely chopped pieces that become crisp during baking.
Potato skins are frequently garnished with green onions or sour cream for flavor contrast.
The dish is popular in bars and pubs as classic comfort food.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Protein from bacon
items.content: Bacon provides protein needed for tissue repair, though it should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Hard cheese is a good source of calcium, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: B vitamins
items.content: Potatoes and bacon contain vitamins B6 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Fiber in the skin
items.content: Potato skin contains dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Bacon and added salt can lead to excess sodium, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Bacon and cheese contain saturated fats, which should be limited in heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to dairy proteins may react to the cheese.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively high in calories, so portion size should be moderate, especially for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the potato skins hot, topped with extra cheese, bacon, and chopped green onions. They are easy to eat with hands as a snack or as a side to meat dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked skins in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 2–3 days. Reheat in the oven to restore crispness. Do not leave them at room temperature for more than a few hours, as they will become soggy.

rice-brown-with-cheese-and-or-cream-base.title: Brown Rice with Cheese and/or Cream Based Sauce, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain product obtained from unprocessed rice kernels. In this version it is served with a cheese‑ and/or cream‑based sauce, but without any added fat, preserving its nutritional value while keeping the dish light.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ layers, providing more fiber and micronutrients than white rice.
Cheese sauce adds calcium and protein, while cream contributes vitamin D and vitamin A when dairy cream is used.
A dish without added fat is suitable for calorie‑restricted diets yet remains flavorful thanks to the natural fats in cheese and cream.
Brown rice has a lower glycemic index than white rice, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.
In some Asian cuisines, rice is traditionally served with a cottage‑cheese‑based sauce, creating a creamy texture without the need for added oil.

items.title: High in Fiber
items.content: The bran layer of brown rice provides soluble and insoluble fiber that supports healthy digestion and satiety.

items.title: Source of Magnesium and Selenium
items.content: Magnesium aids muscle and nerve function, while selenium offers antioxidant protection.

items.title: Calcium from Cheese
items.content: The cheese sauce contributes a substantial amount of calcium, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Combined Plant and Dairy Protein
items.content: Together, rice and cheese deliver a complete amino acid profile useful for tissue repair.

items.title: Low Added Fat Content
items.content: Absence of extra oil reduces overall calories, making the meal suitable for weight‑management plans.

items.title: Lactose Intolerance
items.content: Cheese and cream sauces may cause discomfort for individuals who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: Dairy Allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to cheese or cream.

items.title: Phytic Acid Load
items.content: Brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption if consumed in very large amounts.

items.title: Potential High Sodium
items.content: If the sauce is seasoned with salt, monitor intake to avoid excessive sodium consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice hot, drizzled with the cheese or cream sauce. Garnish with fresh herbs, spices, or vegetables for extra flavor. It works well as a side dish to meat or fish, or as a light main course on its own.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry brown rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice with sauce should be refrigerated and consumed within 2‑3 days, reheating to at least 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned shrimp are peeled and deveined marine crustaceans packed in a sealed tin with brine or oil. They retain a delicate sea flavor, are shelf‑stable, and ready to use in salads, appetizers, pastas, and soups.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shrimp are one of the most consumed seafood items worldwide, with over 150 million tonnes harvested each year.
Canning extends the shelf life of shrimp up to three years while preserving taste and texture.
The majority of canned shrimp come from Asian producers, especially Thailand, Vietnam, and India.
Shrimp are high in protein but low in calories – about 70 kcal per 100 g of product.
Brine often contains citric acid to keep the shrimp pink and fresh‑tasting.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Shrimp provide roughly 20 g of high‑quality protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many seafoods, canned shrimp contain very little saturated fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium is a potent antioxidant that aids immune function and thyroid health.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for red blood cell formation and nervous system maintenance.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids in shrimp help lower triglycerides and improve vascular tone.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp, including anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Canned shrimp are often packed in salty brine, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Heavy metal residues
items.content: Seafood can accumulate cadmium and mercury; choose reputable brands that test for contaminants.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Certain cans may contain preservatives or flavor enhancers that some sensitive individuals prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned shrimp can be eaten straight from the jar, tossed into salads, mixed with pasta, added to rice dishes, or used as a topping for sandwiches. For extra flavor, quickly sauté them with garlic and lemon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened can in a cool, dry place. Once opened, transfer shrimp to an airtight container and refrigerate, consuming within 2–3 days.
